---
title: "Dynamic Programming and Decision Making"
description: "Six tools for problems that ask for the best answer: dynamic programming, memoization, greedy choices, game theory, minimax and bitmasks, with a reading order, a which-tool-when table and a cheat sheet of formulas with worked numbers."
---

Every topic in this group answers a question of the form *"what is the best I can do?"*: the fewest coins, the most meetings, the shortest tour, the biggest lead over an opponent. Trying every possibility is almost always far too slow, because the possibilities multiply. These six tools are six ways to avoid trying them all.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Explain it like I'm ten

Imagine climbing a big hill and wanting the easiest path.

- **Dynamic programming** is writing on a map, at every spot, the easiest way to reach it, starting from the bottom. To fill in a new spot you only look at the spots just below it, which are already written.
- **Memoization** is the same map filled in lazily: you only work a spot out when someone asks, and you write it down so you never work it out twice.
- **Greedy** is always taking the step that looks easiest right now. Sometimes that is perfect; sometimes it walks you into a dead end, so you must check.
- **Game theory** is for when a friend takes turns with you: a spot is good for you if you can send your friend to a spot that is bad for them.
- **Minimax** is assuming your friend will always pick the worst step for you, and choosing so that even then you do as well as possible.
- **Bitmask** is a row of light switches that records which places you have already visited, squeezed into one number, so a map can have one box for every combination.
:::

## Reading order, from simple to advanced

1. **[Dynamic Programming](../dynamic-programming/index.qmd)**: the five steps (state, transition, base case, evaluation order, answer), from stairs to knapsack, LCS, LIS and Burst Balloons.
2. **[Memoization](../memoization/index.qmd)**: the same recurrences written top-down, with exact call counts (2,692,537 against 59 for `fib(30)`) and how to choose the memo key.
3. **[Greedy](../greedy/index.qmd)**: when one choice per step is provably optimal, the exchange argument, and counterexamples such as coins $1, 3, 4$.
4. **[Game Theory](../game-theory/index.qmd)**: winning and losing positions, Nim's XOR rule, Sprague–Grundy values, and games with draws.
5. **[Minimax](../minimax/index.qmd)**: game trees, the score-difference table, and alpha–beta pruning down to about $2\,b^{d/2}$ leaves.
6. **[Bitmask](../bitmask/index.qmd)**: sets as integers, submask enumeration in $3^n$, and dynamic programming over subsets such as Held–Karp.

Read 1 and 2 together: they are one idea seen from two ends. Greedy comes next because the best way to understand it is to compare it with dynamic programming on the same problem. Game theory and minimax add an opponent. Bitmask comes last because its dynamic programs combine everything before it.

## Which tool when

| If the problem says… | Reach for… | Because… |
| --- | --- | --- |
| "count the ways", "fewest", "most", and choices overlap | [Dynamic Programming](../dynamic-programming/index.qmd) | small subproblems repeat; solve each once in a table |
| the recurrence is easy to write but the evaluation order is not, or most states are never needed | [Memoization](../memoization/index.qmd) | the recursion finds the order and visits only reachable states |
| "schedule the most", "fewest jumps", "minimum cost to connect" | [Greedy](../greedy/index.qmd) | one sort and one pass, if an exchange argument proves the rule |
| "two players play optimally; who wins?" | [Game Theory](../game-theory/index.qmd) | a position wins exactly when some move reaches a losing one |
| "maximise your score minus the opponent's", "guarantee the best worst case" | [Minimax](../minimax/index.qmd) | value is the max over your moves of the min over the replies |
| $n \le 20$ and the state is "which items are used" | [Bitmask](../bitmask/index.qmd) | a set fits in one `int`, so it can index a table of $2^n$ entries |
| several independent games are played at once | [Game Theory](../game-theory/index.qmd) | XOR the Grundy values of the parts |
| a game tree too big to search fully | [Minimax](../minimax/index.qmd) with alpha–beta | good move ordering cuts $b^d$ leaves to about $2\,b^{d/2}$ |

## Cheat sheet

**Dynamic programming.**

$$
\text{DP}(s) = \operatorname{opt}_{p \in \text{Pred}(s)} \big( \text{DP}(p) \otimes w(p, s) \big)
$$

where $s$ is a state, $\text{Pred}(s)$ the smaller states it is built from, $\operatorname{opt}$ is $\min$, $\max$ or $\sum$, and $w(p, s)$ the cost of the last decision, combined by $\otimes$ (usually $+$). Example: house robber on $2, 7, 9, 3, 1$ uses $B(i) = \max(B(i-1), B(i-2) + a_i)$: $B = 2, 7, 11, 11, 12$, so the answer is 12.

**Memoization.**

$$
C_{\text{plain}}(n) = 2F(n+1) - 1, \qquad C_{\text{memo}}(n) = 2n - 1
$$

where $C(n)$ is the number of calls made by a recursive Fibonacci function on input $n$, and $F(m)$ is the $m$-th Fibonacci number with $F(1) = F(2) = 1$. Example: for $n = 30$, $C_{\text{plain}} = 2 \times 1{,}346{,}269 - 1 = 2{,}692{,}537$ and $C_{\text{memo}} = 59$.

**Greedy.**

$$
a_t \in \arg\max_{a \in A_t} g(a), \qquad f(g_1) \le f(o_1) \implies (O \setminus \lbrace o_1 \rbrace) \cup \lbrace g_1 \rbrace \text{ is still optimal}
$$

where $a_t$ is the choice at step $t$ from the allowed set $A_t$ by score $g$; in interval scheduling $g_1$ is the greedy first interval, $o_1$ the first interval of an optimal schedule $O$, and $f$ the end time. Example: requests A (1–4), B (3–5), D (5–7), F (8–10): the optimal $\lbrace \text{B}, \text{D}, \text{F} \rbrace$ becomes $\lbrace \text{A}, \text{D}, \text{F} \rbrace$, since A ends at $4 \le 5$. Counterexample: coins $1, 3, 4$ and amount 6 give greedy $4 + 1 + 1$ (3 coins) against $3 + 3$ (2 coins).

**Game theory.**

$$
\text{win}(s) \iff \exists\, s' \in \operatorname{Moves}(s) : \neg\,\text{win}(s'), \qquad \text{Nim is lost for the mover} \iff h_1 \oplus \dots \oplus h_k = 0
$$

where $s$ is a position, $\operatorname{Moves}(s)$ the positions one move away, $h_i$ the Nim heap sizes and $\oplus$ XOR. Example: $3 \oplus 4 \oplus 5 = 011 \oplus 100 \oplus 101 = 010 = 2 \ne 0$, so the first player wins, by shrinking the 3 to $3 \oplus 2 = 1$.

**Minimax.**

$$
V = \max_{a} \min_{b} U(a, b), \qquad L_{\alpha\beta}^{\text{best}} = b^{\lceil d/2 \rceil} + b^{\lfloor d/2 \rfloor} - 1
$$

where $U(a, b)$ is your score after your move $a$ and the reply $b$, and $L_{\alpha\beta}^{\text{best}}$ is the number of leaves alpha–beta examines on a perfectly ordered tree with $b$ moves per position and depth $d$. Example: worst cases $\min(4, 6, 5) = 4$, $\min(7, 2, 9) = 2$ and $\min(3, 8, 1) = 1$ give $V = 4$; for $b = 10$ and $d = 6$, $10^3 + 10^3 - 1 = 1{,}999$ leaves instead of $10^6$.

**Bitmask.**

$$
\operatorname{mask}(S) = \sum_{i \in S} 2^i, \qquad T_{\text{Held–Karp}}(n) = 2^n n^2
$$

where $S$ is a set of items numbered from 0, and $T$ counts the steps of the travelling-salesman dynamic program over (visited set, current stop) on $n$ stops. Example: $\lbrace 0, 2, 3 \rbrace \mapsto 1 + 4 + 8 = 13 = $ `1101`; and $n = 16$ needs $65{,}536 \times 256 \approx 16.8$ million steps, against $15! \approx 1.3 \times 10^{12}$ orders.

## How the topics connect

- A **memoized** recursion and a **dynamic-programming** table compute the same values; the [Memoization](../memoization/index.qmd) lesson counts the calls of one and the [Dynamic Programming](../dynamic-programming/index.qmd) lesson fills the cells of the other.
- **Greedy** is dynamic programming in which only one predecessor ever matters. The coin system $1, 3, 4$ shows what happens when that is not true, and the coin-change table fixes it.
- **Game theory** and **minimax** are dynamic programs over positions with an opponent: the table $D(i, j) = \max(a_i - D(i+1, j),\ a_j - D(i, j-1))$ in [Minimax](../minimax/index.qmd) is the same kind of interval table as Burst Balloons.
- **Bitmask** dynamic programs are dynamic programs whose state contains a set; Held–Karp is the classic example.
